rv.q: Stereophonic is constructed out of those hypernaturalistic details, with each little frustration along the way to an album building on the next, like a fugue, up to the points when those songs start to come together, the play breaks open, and, against all indications, incandescent art comes out.
But they cannot make up for the slackness of the play, which fundamentally adds up to a moderately sudsy and soporific trawl through that familiar trinity: sex, drugs and rock ’n’ roll.
This is an exquisite fantasia on the creation of the now-legendary rock masterpiece known as Rumours.
The three-hour running time zooms by.
Stereophonic is a must-experience, rather than simply a must-see.
Stereophonic is a unique and singular exploration of the passion and torment that comes with making art that passes the test of time, and I have little doubt that this play will, too.
Daniel Aukin’s production of the work could not be more immaculate.
In terms of fresh ideas about the creative process, the play doesn’t deliver an LP’s worth of insights.

rv.q: But while the play breathes, settles, lives most in the studio, there’s not that much process to it, either.
But why we have to be locked in here for over three hours, only Adjmi knows.
Stereophonic has been extended through Dec. 17 at Playwrights Horizons (416 West 42nd St.).

cn.t: Critics praise this Fleetwood Mac-inspired drama for its technical dazzle and Will Butler's music, though most find Adjmi's three-hour deep dive into 1970s studio recording overlong and dramatically thin.

vr.q: I love this play. I cannot recommend it enough.
Last night I saw Stereophonic at Playwrights Horizons and it was amazing
